title: Fossil-parity olefins and liquid fuels from carbon dioxide

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an industrial process that turns captured carbon dioxide into a specified olefin, such as ethene, or a liquid fuel at a cost competitive with producing the same product from fossil feedstocks. Low-carbon electricity or hydrogen would supply the energy needed to convert CO2 into useful molecules. Success requires an integrated production process, including feed preparation, reaction, product recovery and recycling of unconverted material.

The supplied experimental evidence concerns ethene, also called ethylene. Copper-based CO2 electrolysis can join carbon atoms into this two-carbon molecule. Huang and colleagues report an indium/copper membrane electrode assembly operating with high-pressure captured CO2; their calculations and operando studies link enhanced carbon–carbon coupling to pressure-dependent changes in how adsorbed carbon monoxide binds at the catalyst. This provides a concrete technical route toward one product within the broader concept.

The concept is defined by the delivered product and its economics, rather than by a requirement that one device make every olefin and fuel. An economically competitive ethylene process could establish a first realization. Extending that achievement to propene or a specified liquid fuel would require its own evidence of selective synthesis, recovery, durability and cost.

significance.text: As a consequence of the proposed capability, competitive CO2 conversion could change the carbon feedstock used for major chemicals and fuels. Olefins underpin many plastics and chemical intermediates, while liquid hydrocarbons serve fuel markets. Producing these existing commodities from captured CO2 could allow some manufacturing to shift away from petroleum and natural-gas-derived feedstocks while continuing to supply familiar molecules. This is a conditional industrial implication; the supplied ethylene result does not establish adoption or displacement of existing plants.

The process could also store electrical energy in chemical products. Its practical value would depend strongly on electricity price, conversion efficiency and plant utilization. The supplied supplement explores economics under favorable assumptions, including a low-cost renewable-electricity scenario in Saudi Arabia. That scenario illustrates a possible route to competitiveness, rather than establishing competitiveness across locations or electricity markets.

Point-source captured CO2 could support an initial industry without requiring direct air capture. Air-derived CO2 would broaden the feedstock base if capture became sufficiently economical. Climate benefit would remain conditional on the complete life cycle: the energy supply, capture and conditioning requirements, carbon losses, displaced production and eventual fate of the product all matter. Fuel use returns its carbon to the atmosphere, so converting captured CO2 into fuel does not by itself constitute permanent carbon removal.

The analogy to a general electrified commodity platform has limits. An ethylene electrolyzer does not automatically provide ammonia, aromatics, finished polymers or a complete liquid-fuel portfolio. High laboratory current density also does not by itself establish the economics needed to replace steam crackers. Broader product coverage and industrial displacement are downstream possibilities that require additional achievements.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unresolved integrated capability is to deliver a specified commodity competitively while maintaining product selectivity, full-cell energy efficiency, effective carbon utilization, large active electrode area and long operating life on a characterized captured-CO2 feed. These are proposed industrial objectives for this entry, rather than a source-defined checklist. Improving one metric can leave the overall process uneconomic; for example, high selectivity alone does not reveal electricity consumption, carbon losses or replacement costs.

Carbonate and bicarbonate chemistry and salt precipitation are concrete engineering concerns supported by the supplied evidence. Huang and colleagues report that high pressure mitigates salt precipitation by changing where bicarbonate forms near the catalyst–membrane interface. The supplementary caption for a separate experiment at 1 A cm⁻² documents periodic cathode flushing every 12 hours. That intervention identifies a maintenance requirement at that operating condition; it should not be assigned to the reported 600 mA cm⁻² longevity experiment without further evidence.

Energy performance must be assessed across the full cell and supporting process. The supplement reports cell voltage, includes full-cell energy-efficiency calculations and models sensitivity to electricity cost. This makes electrical consumption a central variable in the proposed breakthrough. The earlier research also identified flooding and losses associated with the oxygen-evolution anode as possible barriers, but the supplied review does not independently establish their severity or show that they dominate this system. They remain questions to quantify rather than demonstrated explanations of the remaining gap.

A further engineering challenge is to preserve performance when reaction, separation, compression, recycle and maintenance are combined at larger scale. The feed specification matters: successful operation with high-pressure captured CO2 does not establish tolerance to every capture stream, dilute gas mixture or impurity. The broader concept also requires product-specific chemistry beyond ethylene before claims about propene or liquid fuels can be made.

current_state.text: Huang, Gao, Zhao and colleagues reported conversion of gas-phase, high-pressure captured CO2 to ethylene in an indium/copper membrane electrode assembly in Nature Catalysis 8, 968–976, published 28 August 2025, DOI 10.1038/s41929-025-01411-9. The abstract reports up to 85% ethylene Faradaic efficiency and 750 mA cm⁻² ethylene partial current density under 20 bar. Faradaic efficiency describes the fraction of electrical charge directed to the product; it is distinct from overall energy efficiency. The reported maxima should not be assumed to describe one simultaneous operating point.

The abstract also reports stable electrolysis for more than 1,500 hours at 600 mA cm⁻². Supplementary Table 3 lists the work at 2.75 V, 600 mA cm⁻², 85% ethylene Faradaic efficiency and duration above 1,500 hours. This supplies full-cell voltage information and corroborates the reported longevity result. It does not establish measured plant-scale energy consumption per tonne, manufacturing scale or fossil-route cost parity.

As a proof of concept, recapturing residual CO2 produced a stream reported as 99.9% ethylene. This demonstrates a product-purification result beyond electrochemical selectivity alone. The reported bulk purity does not independently certify compliance with every trace-impurity requirement for polymer-grade ethylene. The feed was high-pressure captured CO2; the supplied material does not establish direct operation on air.

The supplement includes full-cell energy-efficiency calculations and a techno-economic model. Its capital estimates for the electrolyzer and pressure-swing adsorption unit are explicitly optimistic, and one electricity-price scenario uses low-cost renewable power in Saudi Arabia. These calculations explore economic feasibility under stated assumptions. They are not an operating record of a plant selling product at fossil-parity cost.

The supplied review describes partial access to the main article through an abstract preview, alongside a fully extracted supplementary PDF. Consequently, the evidence is broader than an abstract alone, but the complete main text was not available in the retained material. The abstract does not specify electrode area or single-pass conversion of a dilute feed; those omissions do not establish that the electrode was necessarily laboratory-sized. The supplied evidence supports the dated 2025 achievements, while neither demonstrating the proposed integrated industrial target nor resolving whether another group had achieved it by 1 November 2026. No freshness-search record was supplied.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed convincing demonstration: operate a multi-cell stack with individual active electrode areas of at least one square meter for several thousand hours on a characterized captured-CO2 feed, delivering polymer-grade ethene or a specified liquid fuel. Publish the feed composition, pressure, product specification, operating conditions, availability, degradation, maintenance and component replacements. The area and duration thresholds are proposed tests for this record, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Multi-cell stack runs several thousand hours with ≥1 m² electrodes

completion_criteria.text: Publish measured electricity consumption per tonne of saleable product and a complete carbon balance, including unconverted CO2, carbonate-related transfers, by-products, recycle, purges and losses. Use consistent system boundaries for capture or feed conditioning, compression, electrolysis, separation and product finishing. Faradaic efficiency alone would not satisfy this demonstration because it does not establish full-process energy use, carbon utilization, product quality or durability.
completion_criteria.label: Report measured electricity per saleable tonne and complete carbon balance

completion_criteria.text: A transparent cost comparison should show production at or below a specified fossil route at the same site, using consistent assumptions for electricity, capital, utilization, maintenance, financing and product quality. Distinguish measured operating inputs from modeled capital costs and future cost reductions, and disclose the role of subsidies or credits. The comparison should identify the electricity-price and utilization ranges over which parity holds. Any claimed climate benefit should be supported separately by a life-cycle carbon assessment.
completion_criteria.label: Production costs match or undercut a specified same-site fossil route

completion_criteria.text: Independent replication or independently verified operation should establish that the integrated result is reproducible. Tests across explicitly bounded feed compositions, operating loads and maintenance intervals would demonstrate practical breadth. A finite campaign would establish performance within those tested conditions, rather than universal tolerance to captured-CO2 feeds. Completion for one specified product would not establish the whole olefin and liquid-fuel portfolio, and there is no requirement to exceed 90% Faradaic efficiency for every commodity simultaneously.
completion_criteria.label: Integrated performance is independently reproduced or verified within tested conditions

related_concepts.text: Editorial scope comparison: CHE-01, ambient nitrogen fixation, shares the ambition of replacing an established commodity-production route with an efficient, durable alternative, but addresses nitrogen chemistry and ammonia rather than carbon–carbon coupling. CHE-02, direct methane oxidation to methanol, also changes how a commodity molecule is made, but begins with methane and seeks selective oxidation; CHE-03 begins with captured CO2 and requires reduction and, for olefins, carbon–carbon bond formation.

Editorial scope comparison: CHE-04, plant-scale molecular separations, could help with product recovery, CO2 recycle and energy consumption in a CHE-03 process. Separation performance alone would not establish competitive CO2 conversion. CHE-05, first-time-right scale-up of multiphase reactors, overlaps the challenge of preserving transport, selectivity and stability at larger scale, but concerns a broader predictive scale-up capability rather than a particular CO2-derived product.

Editorial scope comparison: CHE-06, direct solar manufacture of fuels and chemicals, overlaps the products and energy-storage goal. Its distinguishing feature is direct solar conversion, whereas CHE-03 is defined by fossil-parity production from CO2 and can use separately generated electricity or hydrogen. CHE-07, closed-loop monomers from mixed plastic waste, seeks useful chemical feedstocks through recovery of existing polymer carbon; CHE-03 introduces captured CO2 as the carbon feedstock. Neither capability establishes the other.

Editorial scope comparison: CHE-08, land-free staple calories from CO2 and renewable energy, shares the use of CO2 and energy to create valuable carbon-containing products, but targets food production with distinct biological, nutritional and processing requirements. CHE-09, direct air capture, could supply atmospheric CO2 to CHE-03. Capture and conversion remain separate achievements, and point-source captured CO2 is sufficient for the proposed initial conversion demonstration.

Editorial scope comparison: CHE-10, on-demand manufacturing of arbitrary small molecules, concerns broad synthetic versatility. CHE-03 instead targets economical, sustained production of specified high-volume olefins or fuels. A successful ethylene process would demonstrate a valuable product-specific capability without establishing arbitrary synthesis. These roster distinctions are editorial boundaries, not findings attributed to the ethylene paper.

unresolved_issues: Whether the proposed integrated industrial capability had been demonstrated elsewhere by 1 November 2026 remains unresolved because no freshness-search record was supplied.
Electrode area, dilute-feed single-pass conversion, feed-impurity tolerance and integrated plant performance are not established by the supplied review.
The relationship among all reported performance maxima is not fully established; they should not be treated as simultaneous without operating-point evidence.
The inspected evidence does not establish measured plant-scale energy consumption per tonne or fossil-parity production cost under consistent site-specific boundaries.
Compliance with every polymer-grade ethylene impurity specification remains unverified despite the reported 99.9% purity.
The relative importance of flooding and oxygen-evolution losses in the reported system remains unverified.
Moore et al., Joule 7, 782–796 (2023), was identified through Huang et al.'s reference list, but its methods, findings and applicability were not inspected.
Propene and liquid-fuel production, air-derived feedstock operation and complete life-cycle climate benefits require evidence beyond the demonstrated ethylene assembly.

brief.title: Affordable chemicals and fuels from captured carbon
possible: The plastics and fuels people use could start with captured carbon dioxide instead of oil or natural gas, at a competitive production cost. Low-carbon electricity or hydrogen would supply the energy to turn that gas into useful molecules.
why: Chemical manufacturers could change their raw material while continuing to supply familiar products. Ethylene, a chemical used to make plastics, offers a first target.
The process could also store electrical energy in chemicals and fuels, giving electricity another route into industries that use carbon-based products.

sources.who: Liang Huang, Ge Gao, Jiwu Zhao and colleagues
sources.showed: They used electricity to turn captured carbon dioxide under high pressure into ethylene. Their system sustained operation and produced a purified ethylene stream.
sources.quote: High pressure also mitigates salt precipitation by relocating bicarbonate formation to the catalyst–membrane interface
sources.cited_for: The work supports sustained ethylene production and purification from captured carbon dioxide.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate an integrated industrial process delivering ethylene at a cost competitive with fossil production.

sources.who: Mingwei Fang, Zihao Huang, Meiling Wang and colleagues
sources.showed: Their water-repelling copper electrode sustained ethylene production without salt buildup. They also tested a stack of reaction cells and feeds containing impurities.
sources.quote:
and operates for over 1,000 hours in a membrane 
electrode assembly  electrolyzer.
sources.cited_for: The work supports longer operation without salt buildup and tolerance to some feed impurities.
sources.not_established: It does not establish sustained operation with industrial electrode areas or competitive costs for a complete production process.

sources.who: Ke Xie, Rui Kai Miao, Adnan Ozden and colleagues
sources.showed: They built a reaction cell that regenerates carbon dioxide from dissolved salts near the reaction surface. This increased the share of incoming gas used in a single pass.
sources.quote: We report a single-pass CO 2 utilization of 78%
sources.cited_for: The work shows a route to reducing carbon losses and the energy needed to separate unused gas.
sources.not_established: Better use of incoming carbon dioxide does not establish complete-process energy consumption, industrial durability or competitive costs.

sources.who: Hakhyeon Song and colleagues at Georgia Tech and DOW Chemical Company
sources.showed: In a preprint, they made ethylene directly from a carbon capture solution. Only 10% of the electrical charge went into ethylene.
sources.quote:
Here, we demonstrate experimentally how a bipolar membrane (BPM) membrane electrode 
assembly (MEA) electrolysis cell can convert CO2 released from carbon capture solutions 
(K2CO3) directly into ethylene (C2H4).
sources.cited_for: The work connects carbon capture solutions directly to ethylene production while exposing an energy-efficiency challenge.
sources.not_established: The low share of charge producing ethylene leaves a large energy requirement and does not establish competitive production.

shown: Huang and colleagues turned high-pressure captured carbon dioxide into ethylene using electricity and sustained operation for more than 1,500 hours. They also demonstrated product purification.
Fang and colleagues demonstrated a water-repelling electrode that avoided salt buildup during prolonged operation. They also tested a small stack of reaction cells and feeds containing impurities.
missing: A large stack must sustain production of a saleable product while accounting for maintenance, degradation and component replacement.
A complete process must measure electricity use per saleable tonne and account for all incoming and outgoing carbon.
Production costs must match a specified fossil process at the same site under consistent assumptions.
Independent testing must reproduce the integrated result across defined feed compositions and operating conditions.

milestones.label: Large electrodes sustain production for thousands of hours
milestones.explanation: A stack with electrodes of at least a square metre would have to deliver plastics-grade ethylene or a specified fuel for several thousand hours on a defined captured-carbon feed. This tests scale and durability.

milestones.label: Measured electricity use and a complete carbon balance
milestones.explanation: The full process would have to report measured electricity per saleable tonne and account for every carbon stream, including recycling and losses. This reveals the resources needed to deliver usable product.

milestones.label: Production costs match a local fossil process
milestones.explanation: A transparent comparison would have to show costs matching or beating a specified fossil process at the same site, with measured inputs and financial assumptions explicit. This establishes where competitive production holds.

milestones.label: Independent testing confirms integrated performance
milestones.explanation: Independent replication or verification would have to confirm integrated performance across defined feeds, operating loads and maintenance intervals. This establishes reproducibility within the tested conditions.

uncertain: Whether durability, efficient energy use, carbon retention and product quality can hold together at industrial scale remains open.
The reported ethylene purity does not establish compliance with every trace-impurity limit for making plastics.
Climate benefit depends on the full production cycle and product use; burning the fuel returns its carbon to the atmosphere.

page.title: CO₂-to-ethylene electrolysis below fossil-route cost
page.definition: An integrated electrochemical process converts captured CO₂ into saleable ethylene (ethene), a feedstock for polyethylene, at a lower levelized production cost than a specified fossil route. Levelized cost includes annualized capital and operating expenses per tonne of product.

goal.need: A 2025 assessment estimated CO₂-to-ethylene electrolysis costs at about 12–26 times those of fossil steam cracking. It compared a 10 MW electrolyser with fossil plants producing 1 million tonnes annually. The difference quantifies the production-cost premium that this route must overcome to supply the same chemical commodity.

figures.caption: Modeled base-case ethylene production costs in a 2025 assessment.
figures.note: These are modeled costs at different plant scales, not measured operating-plant costs.

statements.body: U.S. Department of Energy, Clean Fuels & Products Shot
statements.quote: Decarbonize the fuel and chemical industry through alternative sources of carbon
We provide the first route towards low-carbon footprint ethylene, cost-competitive with fossil
statements.context: The developer’s stated commercial proposition; this passage does not establish operating-plant cost parity.

completion.title: An operating CO₂-to-ethylene process costs less per tonne than a specified fossil route.
completion.criterion: An operating integrated CO₂-to-ethylene process has positive incremental cost reduction: LCOP(fossil) − LCOP(CO₂) > US$0 per tonne of same-grade ethylene, using NETL’s metric. LCOP is annualized capital plus fixed and variable operating costs, including CO₂ supply, electricity, consumables, separation and recycle, divided by annual saleable output. Compare a specified fossil route using consistent location, dollar-year, financing and coproduct assumptions. Establish inputs from plant operation, including maintenance and replacements, rather than assumed future performance. Report subsidies and tax credits separately.
completion.set_by: U.S. DOE/NETL, Basis for Techno-Economic Analysis – Carbon Utilization Procurement Grants, sections 3.3.4 and 3.5.3.4; a general carbon-conversion economic criterion applied here to ethylene.
completion.threshold_quote: This metric needs to have a positive value to show there is a cost saving to be had in replacing the traditional process.
completion.basis: NETL defines incremental cost reduction as traditional-process cost minus new-process cost and requires a positive value to demonstrate savings. Its threshold supplies the economic comparison. Applying it to an operating, integrated ethylene process distinguishes demonstrated production costs from scenarios that assume future equipment performance or prices.

milestones.title: CO₂-to-ethylene electrolysis demonstrates its conversion function in the laboratory.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate the critical conversion function experimentally, corresponding to DOE technology readiness level 3. Xie et al., published 24 June 2022, reported 42% ethylene Faradaic efficiency at 200 mA cm⁻² and 3.82 V. Faradaic efficiency is the fraction of charge producing ethylene. Exposed cathode areas were 3.1–4.2 cm²; the paper states that error bars represent standard deviations from three measurements. This establishes laboratory conversion, not integrated production economics.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations, Multi-Year Program Plan, Table 4.1, TRL 3; the criterion is stated in a table.

milestones.title: Linked CO₂ enrichment and ethylene electrolysis operate for 1,000 hours at 200 mA cm⁻².
milestones.criterion: Connect electrochemical CO₂ enrichment and CO₂-to-ethylene electrolysis in series; run continuously for 1,000 hours at 200 mA cm⁻² and 50% current utilization efficiency. This is NEDO’s laboratory-system target. Fang et al., first published 18 December 2025, ran a separate electrolyser for 1,020 hours at 200 mA cm⁻² and about 68% ethylene Faradaic efficiency, with periodic anion-exchange-membrane replacement. Song et al.’s 21 August 2023 preprint converted capture solution for 24 hours at 10% ethylene Faradaic efficiency. Neither result demonstrates the specified enrichment–electrolysis system.
milestones.set_by: NEDO Moonshot Goal 4, Integrated Electrochemical Systems for Scalable CO2 Conversion to Chemical Feedstocks, Annual Report 2021, page 4; target for its linked electrochemical enrichment and reduction architecture.
milestones.threshold_quote: (Target continuous operation time: 1,000 hours, current density: 200 mA/cm2, a current utilization efficiency : 50%)

milestones.title: A CO₂-to-ethylene electrolysis stack produces a few kilograms of ethylene per day.
milestones.criterion: A stack reaches the CODE programme’s stated output of a few kilograms of ethylene per day. The published target specifies neither an exact minimum nor a test duration. Fang et al. reported a five-cell stack with 50 cm² total active area, peak ethylene Faradaic efficiency of 71.1% at 500 mA cm⁻², and production exceeding 1.2 litres/hour. Selectivity error bars represent three independent measurements. These results do not establish the CODE mass-output target.
milestones.set_by: German federally funded H2-Reallabor Burghausen, CO₂ Direct Electrolysis to Green Ethylene subproject; stack-demonstrator objective published by Fraunhofer UMSICHT on 16 September 2024.
milestones.threshold_quote: an electrolysis stack that produces ethylene at a rate of a few kilograms per day.

milestones.title: A full-scale CO₂-to-ethylene system demonstrates achievement of end-user specifications.
milestones.criterion: Complete a full-scale CO₂-to-ethylene production system, integrate it into its operational environment, and demonstrate achievement of end-user specifications through testing in simulated and operational scenarios. This is DOE TRL 8, its pre-commercial demonstration stage. It concerns the actual production system, including supporting operations; laboratory cells and small stacks alone do not satisfy it. Technical qualification does not establish the separate economic completion test.
milestones.set_by: U.S. Department of Energy, Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs), definition of TRL 8, updated 18 August 2026; a general system-qualification criterion.
milestones.threshold_quote: All functionality is tested in simulated and operational scenarios with demonstrated achievement of end-user specifications.

not_found: Searches of DOE/NETL, NEDO, RMI and developer disclosures found no public operating-plant cost record establishing fossil-route cost parity for CO₂-derived ethylene.
Public results establishing the complete NEDO linked-system target, CODE stack-output target or full-scale DOE TRL 8 qualification were not found.
Huang et al.’s Nature Catalysis article and its KAUST manuscript could not be opened successfully.
Independent replicate counts for the cited long-duration operating campaigns were not established.
